newsitem.title: USA: Canada and U.S. discuss Pacific salmon dispute.
newsitem.headline: Canada and U.S. discuss Pacific salmon dispute.

text.p: Canada's fisheries minister met the U.S. commerce secretary on Tuesday in a bid to convince him that frustrated Canadian fishermen have valid complaints about salmon overfishing, mainly by Alaskan boats.

"The important point is to recognise here in Washington that there is a basis for their frustration and that is the message I have been carrying," Canadian Fisheries and Oceans Minister David Anderson told reporters.
The dispute over Pacific salmon led to a dramatic three-day blockade of the Alaska state ferry Malaspina last week by 200 Canadian fishing boats in British Columbia.
Anderson said he had "frank and constructive" talks with Commerce Secretary William Daley as well as senators from Alaska. No major decisions were taken to resolve the battle.
Canada claims the U.S. fishing industry is drastically overfishing salmon in violation of the Pacific Salmon Treaty that was signed in 1985.
The United States denies overfishing. Daley said after the meeting he believed U.S. fishing was being conducted responsibly and in a manner consistent with the treaty.

"Minister Anderson and I have committed to a process involving fishermen and others who are active in the fisheries. We both agree this is essential to resolving differences between our two countries," Daley said in a statement.

Last week, both countries appointed special envoys to try and resolve the dispute. William Ruckelshaus, a former head of the Environmental Protection Agency, will lead U.S. efforts while University of British Columbia President and Chancellor David Strangway is the Canadian choice.
Daley said Pacific salmon negotiations were in the best interest of both countries. "We look forward to a reinvigorated negotiating process which is the way to resolve these issues," Daley said.
So-called "salmon interceptions" are at the heart of the dispute.

The salmon begin their life cycle in fresh water and then migrate to the ocean where they grow and mature before returning to their river of origin to spawn. It is on their return inland to either Washington state and Alaska in the United States or British Columbia in Canada that the fish are caught.
Anderson said since the treaty was signed, the U.S. share of Pacific salmon has consistently increased.
"U.S. fishermen are deriving substantially greater benefit than is justified by the production in U.S. rivers," he said.
He dismissed U.S. claims that the salmon harvest was bigger this year and that was why U.S. fishermen were yielding more than in previous years.
"Their numbers just don't add up," Anderson said. "We just have not seen the fish they are talking about."
